sec: Step 3 — compensatory changes, both tables · p828

items.q: Match the metabolic abnormalities to their compensation — 1) Metabolic acidosis  2) Metabolic alkalosis  3) Compensation for metabolic acidosis  4) Compensation for metabolic alkalosis … A) Respiratory acidosis  B) ↓HCO₃⁻ with ↓PaCO₂  C) Respiratory alkalosis  D) ↑HCO₃⁻ with ↑PaCO₂
items.exp: Metabolic acidosis (↓HCO₃⁻, ↓PaCO₂) is compensated by respiratory alkalosis, and metabolic alkalosis (↑HCO₃⁻, ↑PaCO₂) by respiratory acidosis. (Book p828)

items.q: In metabolic acidosis, the direction of the compensatory PaCO₂ change is:
items.exp: Metabolic acidosis table row: HCO₃⁻ ↓, PaCO₂ ↓, compensation = respiratory alkalosis. (Book p828)

items.q: For every 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻, the expected fall in PaCO₂ is:
items.exp: For ↓1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ → ↓1.2 mmHg pCO₂; for ↑1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ → ↑0.7 mmHg pCO₂. (Book p828)

items.q: For every 1 mEq/L rise in HCO₃⁻, the expected rise in PaCO₂ is:
items.exp: For ↑1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ → ↑0.7 mmHg pCO₂ (the metabolic alkalosis compensation rule). (Book p828)

items.q: A patient's HCO₃⁻ falls by 10 mEq/L from normal. Using the printed rule, what PaCO₂ change do you expect?
items.exp: Using ↓1.2 mmHg pCO₂ per 1 mEq/L fall in HCO₃⁻, a 10 mEq/L fall predicts a 12 mmHg fall in PaCO₂. (Book p828)

items.q: Match the respiratory abnormalities to their compensation — 1) Respiratory acidosis  2) Respiratory alkalosis  3) Compensation for respiratory acidosis  4) Compensation for respiratory alkalosis … A) Metabolic alkalosis  B) ↑PaCO₂ with ↑HCO₃⁻  C) Metabolic acidosis  D) ↓PaCO₂ with ↓HCO₃⁻
items.exp: Respiratory acidosis (↑PaCO₂, ↑HCO₃⁻) is compensated by metabolic alkalosis; respiratory alkalosis (↓PaCO₂, ↓HCO₃⁻) by metabolic acidosis. (Book p828)

items.q: For an ACUTE rise in PaCO₂ of 10 mmHg, the expected HCO₃⁻ change is:
items.exp: ↑10 mmHg PaCO₂ → ↑1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ (acute) or ↑4 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ (chronic). (Book p828)

items.q: For a CHRONIC rise in PaCO₂ of 10 mmHg, the expected HCO₃⁻ change is:
items.exp: ↑10 mmHg PaCO₂ → ↑4 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ in the chronic state (versus ↑1 mEq/L acutely). (Book p828)

items.q: Match the fall in PaCO₂ to its HCO₃⁻ change — 1) ↓10 mmHg acute  2) ↓10 mmHg chronic  3) Difference between them … A) ↓2 mEq/L  B) The chronic state compensates more  C) ↓4 mEq/L
items.exp: ↓10 mmHg PaCO₂ → ↓2 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ acutely and ↓4 mEq/L chronically, i.e. the chronic state compensates more. (Book p828)

items.q: A patient with chronic obstructive lung disease has a PaCO₂ 10 mmHg above normal with an HCO₃⁻ 4 mEq/L above normal. What does the table call this?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis with minimal compensation
Acute respiratory alkalosis with an acute fall in HCO₃⁻
items.exp: A 10 mmHg PaCO₂ rise producing a 4 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ rise matches the chronic row; the acute row would give only 1 mEq/L. (Book p828)

items.q: ‘For a fall in PaCO₂ the acute change in HCO₃⁻ (2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg) is larger than the chronic change.’
opts: False — the chronic fall is larger (4 mEq/L per 10 mmHg) than the acute fall (2 mEq/L)
True — 2 mEq/L acute exceeds the 4 mEq/L chronic change
False — an acute fall in PaCO₂ changes HCO₃⁻ by 1 mEq/L
True, and the same is true for a rise in PaCO₂
items.exp: The table prints ↓10 mmHg PaCO₂ → ↓2 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ (acute) and ↓4 mEq/L (chronic): chronic compensation is greater. (Book p828)

items.q: All but one of these step-3 compensation rules are printed. Which is the odd one out?
opts: ↑10 mmHg PaCO₂ raises HCO₃⁻ by 4 mEq/L acutely and 1 mEq/L chronically
↓1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ lowers PaCO₂ by 1.2 mmHg
↑1 mEq/L HCO₃⁻ raises PaCO₂ by 0.7 mmHg
↓10 mmHg PaCO₂ lowers HCO₃⁻ by 2 mEq/L acutely
items.exp: The acute value is 1 mEq/L and the chronic value 4 mEq/L — the option reverses them. (Book p828)
